stem: Distinguish between basic movements and functional movements of the gastrointestinal tract with two examples of each.
options: Basic movements occur along the GIT intrinsically (e.g., peristalsis and deglutition/swallowing), whereas functional movements are elicited by the presence of food in the tract (e.g., mastication/chewing, gastric motility [propulsion and retropulsion], and gastric emptying).

Primary esophageal peristalsis is initiated by the act of swallowing as food enters the esophagus, whereas Secondary esophageal peristalsis is initiated locally by the continued presence/distension of food remaining in the esophagus.

A portal triad consists of a branch of the bile duct, a branch of the hepatic artery, and a branch of the hepatic portal vein. Kupffer cells are macrophages lining liver sinusoids that phagocytose debris and old blood cells.
Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor; Chief (peptic/zymogen) cells secrete pepsinogen (and gastric lipase); D cells secrete somatostatin.

topic: Digestive System I: Gastrointestinal Structure, Accessory Organs, Sphincters and Motility
subtopic: SAQ 1.1
stem: List the four histological layers of the gastrointestinal tract wall from innermost to outermost and state one key structural or functional feature of each.
options: 1. Mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae—secretes mucus, acid, and enzymes and absorbs nutrients); 2. Submucosa (connective tissue housing blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and submucosal glands supporting mucosa); 3. Muscularis Externa (circular and longitudinal smooth muscle—plus inner oblique in stomach—driving mixing and propulsion); 4. Serosa (visceral peritoneum reducing friction and protecting organs).

The small intestine features circular folds, finger-like villi (with blood capillaries and lacteals), and microvilli to maximize surface area for nutrient digestion and absorption. The large intestine has NO villi, instead featuring abundant straight tubular Crypts of Lieberkuhn, numerous mucus-secreting goblet cells for lubrication/protection, immune cells in the lamina propria, haustra, and taenia coli for water/electrolyte absorption and feces formation.

Deglutition: (1) Oral phase (voluntary—tongue forces bolus back against hard palate), (2) Pharyngeal phase (involuntary, 1–2s, medulla/lower pons, inhibits breathing while pushing bolus past open UES), (3) Esophageal phase (involuntary primary/secondary peristalsis to stomach). Receptive relaxation is fundal enlargement accommodating incoming food for storage, whereas retropulsion is the back-and-forth churning of chyme propelled against the closed pyloric sphincter.

1. Upper Esophageal Sphincter (controls bolus entry from pharynx to esophagus); 2. Lower Esophageal/Cardiac Sphincter (prevents gastric acid reflux into esophagus); 3. Pyloric Sphincter (regulates chyme emptying from stomach to duodenum); 4. Sphincter of Oddi (controls bile and pancreatic juice entry into duodenum); 5. Ileocecal Valve (regulates transit from ileum to cecum and prevents backflow); 6. Internal and External Anal Sphincters (control fecal continence and defecation).

topic: Digestive System II: Digestive Juices, Enzymatic Digestion and Nutrient Absorption
subtopic: SAQ 2.1
stem: Explain how sodium-glucose co-transport works at the intestinal enterocyte, specifying the roles of SGLT1, GLUT2, and the Na+/K+-ATPase.
options: Gastric juice (~2 L/day) contains mucus, bicarbonate, HCl, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, and gastrin, secreted across Cephalic (thought/sight/smell/taste), Gastric (stomach distension/pH rise), and Intestinal (duodenal chyme) phases. Brush-border disaccharidases: maltase (maltose -> glucose + glucose), lactase (lactose -> glucose + galactose), and sucrase (sucrose -> glucose + fructose).

The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase uses ATP to actively pump Na+ out of the enterocyte, maintaining an inward Na+ gradient. Apical SGLT1 harnesses this Na+ gradient to cotransport glucose (and galactose) into the enterocyte against its concentration gradient. Intracellular glucose then exits passively across the basolateral membrane via GLUT2 facilitated diffusion into interstitial fluid and hepatic portal capillaries.

Synthesized by hepatocytes and concentrated in the gallbladder, bile salts emulsify large hydrophobic fat globules in the duodenum into tiny droplets, massively increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase + colipase. Bile salts then incorporate fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol into micelles to shuttle them across the unstirred water layer to the brush border. Afterward, bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via the Apical Sodium-Dependent Bile Acid Transporter (ASBT).

Gastrin (pyloric G cells) stimulates gastric HCl secretion and gastric motility. Secretin (duodenal S cells) stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic and ductal secretions to neutralize acidic chyme. CCK (duodenal I cells) stimulates gallbladder contraction, pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion, and slows gastric emptying.

topic: Digestive System II: Digestive Juices, Enzymatic Digestion and Nutrient Absorption
subtopic: SAQ 2.4
stem: State the cellular sources and main gastrointestinal actions of Gastrin, Secretin, and Cholecystokinin (CCK).
options: Gastrin (pyloric G cells) stimulates gastric HCl secretion and gastric motility. Secretin (duodenal S cells) stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic and ductal secretions to neutralize acidic chyme. CCK (duodenal I cells) stimulates gallbladder contraction, pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion, and slows gastric emptying.

Gastric juice (~2 L/day) contains mucus, bicarbonate, HCl, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, and gastrin, secreted across Cephalic (thought/sight/smell/taste), Gastric (stomach distension/pH rise), and Intestinal (duodenal chyme) phases. Brush-border disaccharidases: maltase (maltose -> glucose + glucose), lactase (lactose -> glucose + galactose), and sucrase (sucrose -> glucose + fructose).

The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase uses ATP to actively pump Na+ out of the enterocyte, maintaining an inward Na+ gradient. Apical SGLT1 harnesses this Na+ gradient to cotransport glucose (and galactose) into the enterocyte against its concentration gradient. Intracellular glucose then exits passively across the basolateral membrane via GLUT2 facilitated diffusion into interstitial fluid and hepatic portal capillaries.

Synthesized by hepatocytes and concentrated in the gallbladder, bile salts emulsify large hydrophobic fat globules in the duodenum into tiny droplets, massively increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase + colipase. Bile salts then incorporate fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol into micelles to shuttle them across the unstirred water layer to the brush border. Afterward, bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via the Apical Sodium-Dependent Bile Acid Transporter (ASBT).

topic: Renal System Physiology: Nephron Architecture, Urine Formation, Clearance and Micturition
subtopic: SAQ 3.1
stem: List the six major physiological functions of the renal system and trace arterial blood flow from the renal artery to the glomerular capillary.
options: In juxtamedullary Loops of Henle (Countercurrent Multiplier), water leaves the descending limb while Na+ is actively pumped out of the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, establishing a steep 300 -> 1,200 mOsm medullary interstitial gradient. The Vasa Recta (Countercurrent Exchanger) supplies nutrients without washing away this gradient, allowing ADH-regulated water reabsorption from the collecting duct.

Barrier: (1) Fenestrated capillary endothelium (blocks blood cells), (2) Negatively charged Glomerular Basement Membrane (Type IV collagen/proteoglycans), and (3) Podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms (nephrin/podocin—restricts plasma proteins like albumin/IgG). Four processes: Glomerular filtration (~180 L/day), Tubular reabsorption (~178.5 L/day), Tubular secretion (H+, K+, drugs), and Excretion (~1.5 L/day).

Functions: filter ~180–200 L/day plasma, excrete metabolic wastes/toxins, secrete renin for BP regulation, regulate plasma osmolarity/electrolytes, maintain long-term acid-base balance, and produce erythropoietin for RBCs. Components: (1) Macula Densa (non-innervated thick-ascending-limb chemoreceptors sensing decreased NaCl load), (2) Extraglomerular mesangial/lacis cells, and (3) Renin-producing Granular cells (sympathetically innervated baroreceptors in afferent/efferent arterioles). topic: Reproductive Physiology II: Fertilization, Pregnancy, Placenta, Parturition, Lactation and Fetal Circulation
subtopic: In-Text Self-Check
stem: How many umbilical arteries and umbilical veins connect the fetus to the placenta, and which vessel carries oxygenated blood back to the fetus?
options: Two umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placenta, and one umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood from the placenta back to the fetus.

1. Ductus venosus (bypasses the semi-functional fetal liver); 2. Foramen ovale (shunts right atrial blood to left atrium, bypassing pulmonary circuit); 3. Ductus arteriosus (shunts pulmonary artery blood into aorta, bypassing the non-functional lungs).

The luteal-placental shift (weeks 8–12 of the 1st trimester) is the transition in which the placenta takes over progesterone/estrogen synthesis from the corpus luteum. Syncytiotrophoblast-derived hCG rescues and maintains the corpus luteum prior to this shift.

Physiological anaemia occurs because maternal blood/plasma volume rises (+40–50%) disproportionately faster than red blood cell mass, diluting haemoglobin. Elevated UTI risk results from impaired tubular reabsorption of the heightened filtered glucose load (glycosuria) alongside bladder compression/urinary stasis.

explanation.correct: Two umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placenta, and one umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood from the placenta back to the fetus.

topic: Reproductive Physiology II: Fertilization, Pregnancy, Placenta, Parturition, Lactation and Fetal Circulation
subtopic: SAQ 5.1
stem: Trace the journey from ovulation to blastocyst implantation, explaining the acrosome reaction, cortical reaction, and the four stages of implantation.
options: Ovulation (Day 0) -> ampullary fertilization within 24 hrs: sperm acrosome reaction digests zona pellucida, plasma membranes fuse, and cortical reaction hardens the egg coat against polyspermy -> cleavage (Days 1–3) -> morula (Day 3) -> blastocyst (Day 5). Implantation (Days 6–9) proceeds via Hatching, Apposition (pinopod contact), Adhesion (firm trophoblast binding), Invasion (syncytiotrophoblast penetration), and Decidualization.

Differences: open Foramen Ovale, patent Ductus Arteriosus (parallel ventricular pumping), bypassed non-functional lungs (placenta acts as lungs), and fetal HbF with higher O2 affinity than maternal Hb. Six changes at birth: closure of placental circulation, shutting of foramen ovale, closure of ductus arteriosus, umbilical artery constriction (stress/high O2/cold), spontaneous respiration onset, and marked neonatal haemodynamic shifts.

Placental functions: Respiratory (O2/CO2 exchange), Nutritive (glucose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins), Excretory (urea/creatinine), Endocrine (steroids/peptides), Immunological (tolerance + maternal IgG transfer). hCG (syncytiotrophoblast): rescues corpus luteum/progesterone. hPL (syncytiotrophoblast): induces maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis to feed fetus, aids breast growth. Relaxin (corpus luteum/placenta): cervical remodelling, pelvic ligament relaxation, renal vasodilation.

Near term, rising estrogen, oxytocin receptors, gap junctions, and functional progesterone shift prime the myometrium. Fetal head stretching the cervix sends nerve signals to the hypothalamus -> posterior pituitary releases oxytocin -> stronger uterine contractions -> placenta releases prostaglandins -> greater cervical stretch in a positive-feedback loop. Stages: (1) Cervical dilation (up to ~10 cm), (2) Fetal expulsion (delivery of baby), (3) Placental delivery (expulsion of afterbirth).

Six changes at birth: closure of placental circulation, shutting of foramen ovale, closure of ductus arteriosus, umbilical artery constriction (stress/high O2/cold), spontaneous respiration onset, and marked neonatal haemodynamic shifts.

Ovulation (Day 0) -> ampullary fertilization within 24 hrs: sperm acrosome reaction digests zona pellucida, plasma membranes fuse, and cortical reaction hardens the egg coat against polyspermy -> cleavage (Days 1–3) -> morula (Day 3) -> blastocyst (Day 5). Implantation (Days 6–9) proceeds via Hatching, Apposition (pinopod contact), Adhesion (firm trophoblast binding), Invasion (syncytiotrophoblast penetration), and Decidualization.

Placental functions: Respiratory (O2/CO2 exchange), Nutritive (glucose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins), Excretory (urea/creatinine), Endocrine (steroids/peptides), Immunological (tolerance + maternal IgG transfer). hCG (syncytiotrophoblast): rescues corpus luteum/progesterone. hPL (syncytiotrophoblast): induces maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis to feed fetus, aids breast growth. Relaxin (corpus luteum/placenta): cervical remodelling, pelvic ligament relaxation, renal vasodilation.

Near term, rising estrogen, oxytocin receptors, gap junctions, and functional progesterone shift prime the myometrium. Fetal head stretching the cervix sends nerve signals to the hypothalamus -> posterior pituitary releases oxytocin -> stronger uterine contractions -> placenta releases prostaglandins -> greater cervical stretch in a positive-feedback loop. Stages: (1) Cervical dilation (up to ~10 cm), (2) Fetal expulsion (delivery of baby), (3) Placental delivery (expulsion of afterbirth).

stem: State the Frank-Starling Law of the Heart and distinguish the origin of the 'LUB' and 'DUP' heart sounds.

topic: Cardiovascular Physiology: Cardiac Cycle, Haemodynamics, Conducting System and Electrocardiography
subtopic: SAQ 6.1
stem: Define Stroke Volume, Heart Rate, Cardiac Output, Pulse Pressure, and Blood Pressure, giving the mathematical relationships and normal adult resting values.
options: 1. Excitability: ability to respond to stimulation and generate an impulse; 2. Rhythmicity: ability to discharge impulses continuously and regularly; 3. Conductivity: ability to transmit action potentials across the entire cardiac muscle from one point; 4. Contractility: ability to contract mechanically following electrical excitation.

Stroke Volume (SV): volume pumped per ventricle per beat (~70–72 mL). Heart Rate (HR): beats per minute. Cardiac Output: $Q = SV \times HR$ (rising to 25–35 L/min in exercise). Pulse Pressure = Systolic − Diastolic ($120 - 70 = 50$ mmHg). Blood Pressure (arterial pressure, ~120/70 mmHg) = Cardiac Output $\times$ Peripheral Resistance.

ECGs evaluate excitation events, arrhythmias, cardiac hypertrophy, myocardial damage, and ischaemia/necrosis. The QRS complex (normal duration 0.08 s, ventricular depolarization via AV bundle/Purkinje fibers) consists of a negative Q wave preceding a positive R wave, followed by a negative S wave. The P-R interval normally spans 0.12–0.21 seconds (measuring AV conduction time and nodal delay).

SA Node (pacemaker, 90–120 bpm) -> Bachmann's bundle (interatrial tract causing near-simultaneous left/right atrial depolarization) and Anterior/Middle/Posterior Internodal Tracts (block-resistant conduits to AV node) -> AV Node (100–150 ms delay for ventricular filling) -> Bundle of His & Right/Left Bundle Branches -> Purkinje Fibers (fastest conduction for near-simultaneous ventricular contraction).

stem: Complete this statement about The Conducting System of the Heart: Cardiac excitation originates intrinsically within specialized conducting cells—low in contractility, rich in mitochondria and glycogen, and electrically specialized—arranged across six sequential structures so atria always contract before ventricles: (1) Sinoatrial (SA) Node (the Pacemaker)—located at the posterior upper right atrium near the superior vena cava entrance; fires intrinsically at 90–120 beats/min (higher in youth, declining with age; accelerated by fever, thyroid hormone, epinephrine, and norepinephrine); (2) Interatrial Tract (Bachmann's Bundle)—conducts impulses rapidly from the SA node to the left atrium for near-simultaneous bi-atrial depolarization and contraction; (3) Internodal Tracts (Anterior, Middle, and Posterior bundles)—specialized pathways linking the SA node to the AV node that resist conduction ____ atrial muscle; (4) Atrioventricular (AV) Node—located beneath the right interatrial septal endocardium near the tricuspid valve, serving normally as the SOLE electrical bridge from atria to ventricles and richly innervated by sympathetic and vagal fibers; its slow conduction produces the critical AV Nodal Delay (100–150 milliseconds), giving the atria time to finish emptying blood into the ventricles before ventricular systole; (5) Bundle of His (AV Bundle)—continues from the AV node along the right interventricular septum and splits into Right and Left Bundle Branches; and (6) Purkinje Fibers—extensive subendocardial ventricular branches possessing the HIGHEST conduction velocity in the heart, ensuring near-simultaneous, high-efficiency contraction of both ventricles.

stem: Complete this statement about Cardiovascular Terminologies, Haemodynamics, Cardiac Cycle, and Muscle Properties: Cardiac muscle exhibits four intrinsic properties: (1) Excitability (ability to respond to stimuli and generate impulses), (2) Rhythmicity (automatic continuous, ____), (3) Conductivity (transmission of action potentials across the myocardium), and (4) Contractility (mechanical shortening following electrical excitation).

explanation.correct: Cardiovascular Terminologies, Haemodynamics, Cardiac Cycle, and Muscle Properties: Cardiac muscle exhibits four intrinsic properties: (1) Excitability (ability to respond to stimuli and generate impulses), (2) Rhythmicity (automatic continuous, regular impulse discharge), (3) Conductivity (transmission of action potentials across the myocardium), and (4) Contractility (mechanical shortening following electrical excitation).
